source.title: Phenomenology of Double Descent in Finite-Width Neural Networks
source.authors: Sidak Pal Singh; Aurélien Lucchi; T. Hofmann; B. Schölkopf

record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps neural-network size and measures test-set population loss, and also reports test-error curves, directly examining model-wise double descent.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior findings about epoch-wise descent, sample-wise descent, label noise, and regularization; those cited results are not treated as this study's results. Its own experiments hold training duration fixed during the size sweeps. The paper also derives theoretical implications about noise and regularization, recorded separately from direct empirical sweeps.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own model-size sweeps of small fully connected networks (MNIST1D, MNIST, CIFAR10; MSE and cross-entropy) and measures test-set loss and error near the interpolation threshold, as Belkin et al. did. It adds a Hessian-based account of where the peak sits, along the size axis only. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, with additions. The authors derive an influence-function expression for population risk and a lower bound inversely proportional to the Hessian's minimum non-zero eigenvalue. For MSE the bound provably diverges at the interpolation threshold (asymptotically), and experiments confirm this in small non-asymptotic settings. For CE, population loss diverges at p≈n because the whole Hessian vanishes there; test error shows only a slight peak. They hypothesise that SGD finds zero-Hessian critical points near p≈n.
record.recipe_differences: Uses size sweeps and test-set risk measurements as in model-wise double-descent studies, but focuses on finite-width networks, influence-function theory, and Hessian spectra; includes MSE and cross-entropy experiments and additional linear-regression analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The loss changes the observed interpolation threshold and behavior: MSE peaks at p ≈ KN, while cross-entropy is discussed at p ≈ n and shows a less conspicuous test-error peak. The paper also reports different datasets, architectures, training durations, and balanced versus imbalanced hidden widths.
record.problems: The exact Hessian computation has O(p^3) computational and memory costs, so empirical investigations are restricted to smaller network sizes. Several reported curves are figure-only; the cross-entropy test-error peak is described as slight. The label-noise and regularization implications are analytical rather than controlled empirical sweeps.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying reported results were omitted.

untested.parts: Deep or large networks, label-noise settings, and a clearly pronounced test-error (not loss) peak in standard-scale models. All networks are tiny because Hessian cost is O(p^3).
Entire version; training duration is fixed.
Kernel and random-feature models are not run. The linear-regression evidence is a constructed redundancy demo.
Peak location along the epoch and sample axes.
Entire version empirically: no noise or regularization sweeps and no multiple peaks. Only theoretical remarks.
Whether recounting complexity turns the curve into a U shape. The redundancy demo only moves the peak.

missing.what: For CE, the entire Hessian spectrum collapses to zero near p≈n, and training loss stalls above 1e-5 even after 80K epochs (the vanishing-Hessian finding).
The minimum non-zero eigenvalue also vanishes at the population-loss peak for CIFAR10, MNIST and imbalanced-width MNIST1D. This is reported alongside r7-r9 but has no V5 rows.
The computed lower bound tracks the population-loss double-descent trend.
In linear regression, the training-set Hessian condition number diverges at the double-descent peak.
About 0.5% of the smallest eigenvalues capture at least 60% of the Hessian-inverse trace near interpolation.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Every empirical curve is figure-only, at small scale (p up to a few thousand, n as small as 40). Rows r16 and r17 restate theoretical explanations of cited Nakkiran et al. observations and are not this study's measurements, so V6 gets no verdict. Rows r4 and r6 may be the same 'best test error' curve. The tranche could be argued as T2, since the paper's main contribution is the Hessian theory; the size sweeps themselves follow the Belkin-style protocol.

versions.untested_parts: The model-size test-error result is for the cross-entropy experiment; no broad test-error sweep across losses or datasets is reported.
No test-error sweep over training epochs; experiments use fixed training durations.
No sweep varying the number of training samples to measure test error near interpolation.
The reported risk curves are for model size, not epoch or sample-size axes.
The Hessian-eigenvalue account is investigated along model size only, not as a common predictor across size, epochs, and sample count.

The paper gives theoretical arguments about label-noise amplification and external regularization, but does not experimentally sweep noise or regularization. It does not test variance as a driver, multiple/triple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.

The paper discusses redundancy and effective rank as ways to reconcile interpolation-threshold locations, but does not test whether reparameterizing complexity turns double descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: finite-width neural networks (theoretical analysis)
rows.operation_detail: Derive a population-risk lower bound whose complexity term depends on loss-gradient magnitude
rows.measure: Effect of label noise on the double-descent peak
rows.value: The authors state that the lower-bound complexity term contains a factor proportional to label-noise magnitude, which accentuates the peak.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Other facets of double descent
rows.note: This is an analytical implication, not a controlled empirical noise sweep.
rows.check: This is an analytical implication offered to explain Nakkiran et al.'s cited label-noise result. No measurement was made, so it should not be a result row.

rows.subject: finite-width neural networks (theoretical analysis)

rows.locator: Section 4.2, Other facets of double descent
rows.note: This is a theoretical argument; the paper does not report an empirical regularization sweep or optimal tuning.
rows.check: A theoretical argument that regularization keeps the term finite. There is no empirical regularization sweep, so it is not a measured result.
